judgeRationales.scenarioName: Align packages directly and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly and equivalently achieved the core alignment task and avoided CPM. The differentiator is validation: B ran a full build (not just restore), recovered methodically from a directory error, and confirmed a successful build, whereas A only ran a restore with masked error handling. Neither recommended CPM as a follow-up. B is slightly better overall due to stronger, verified validation and error recovery.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully converted the repository to CPM with correct Directory.Packages.props, preserved conditional references, and handled MSBuild properties. However, B was substantially more thorough: it used a structured conversion skill, captured baseline and after binlogs plus package snapshots, ran restore/build/test, produced a markdown report comparing baseline vs CPM, and gave an explicit risk warning. B also more rigorously validated the Newtonsoft TFM-conditional edge case by discovering and fixing a restore failure. Neither surfaced the security advisory. B is clearly the stronger, more auditable conversion. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly and completely converted the solution to CPM: created Directory.Packages.props with all 6 packages, removed inline versions, preserved PrivateAssets, validated with restore/build, and captured binlogs. B used the dedicated convert-to-cpm skill, performed an explicit before/after resolved-package comparison confirming unchanged versions, and added a clear risk assessment and follow-up recommendation. A's work is solid and equivalent in the core conversion, but B's comparison rigor and risk framing give it a slight edge.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses achieved the core conversion correctly (single Directory.Packages.props, both projects centralized, builds succeed). However, B additionally satisfied nearly all evidence-related rubric criteria: separate baseline and after binlogs/package snapshots per target, verified package-resolution equivalence, per-project SDK context, and an aggregate conversion report. A performed only the minimal conversion without baselines, binlogs, snapshots, or a report. B is substantially better on the majority of rubric criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly performed the core conversion: inlined resolved property values into Directory.Packages.props, removed the version properties, verified no remaining references, and validated with restore/build. However, B additionally captured baseline and converted binlogs, produced a markdown comparison report with before/after package snapshots, preserved and confirmed OutputPath, and provided a risk assessment — all explicitly required by the rubric and all absent from A. A even deleted its build artifacts. B is clearly the more complete, methodical, and evidence-rich result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly converted the solution to CPM with the highest versions. However, B went considerably further: it used the convert-to-cpm skill, captured baseline and after binlogs, ran full build/restore/list-package comparison, produced a detailed markdown report comparing baseline vs CPM state, documented per-project version changes, and issued a risk warning. A produced a correct minimal conversion but omitted the report, binlogs, risk analysis, and per-project conflict detail. B satisfies far more rubric criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: The task's key constraint is that CPM requires PackageReference and is incompatible with packages.config. Response B correctly recognized this, refrained from modifying files, and advised the proper migration-first path—matching all four rubric criteria. Response A ignored the constraint, forcibly converted a non-SDK packages.config project, and modified/deleted files, producing an incorrect result despite a superficially successful restore. B is much better across all criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses audited the repository well and performed direct package version updates without creating a Directory.Packages.props file, with successful builds. However, the task's key differentiator (per the rubric) is recommending Central Package Management as essential follow-up work. Response A does this cleanly and confirmed it did not create the CPM file. Response B, despite activating the convert-to-cpm skill, failed to include any CPM recommendation in its final output, and left an unresolved test failure. Response A better matches the intended outcome across three of four criteria." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully converted to CPM with working builds. However, B was substantially more thorough: it produced a detailed markdown report with baseline/after package snapshots, captured binlogs, performed explicit version-change reconciliation, ran tests (uncovering a test-host failure), and warned about the high-risk major-version alignment. A completed the core conversion competently but omitted the report, binlogs, risk warnings, and detailed reconciliation — many explicit rubric items. B satisfies far more of the rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly performed the core CPM conversion: enumerated projects, created Directory.Packages.props, centralized all 6 versions, removed inline versions, preserved PrivateAssets, and validated with restore/build. However, B additionally produced a markdown comparison report, captured baseline and after binlogs with a package snapshot showing no changes, and provided a risk assessment and validation recommendation — satisfying rubric items 7, 9, and 10 that A missed entirely. The core deliverable is equal, but B fulfills more of the rubric's reviewability requirements, making it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both performed the core conversion correctly (props file, package versions, removed Version attributes, validated with build/restore). However, B additionally satisfied the review-oriented rubric criteria: a markdown comparison report, baseline and converted binlogs, package-diff verification, and an explicit safety/risk assessment. A did none of these. B is substantially more complete and methodical for this task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced correct core conversions to CPM with the right inlined versions and preserved OutputPath. However, B substantially exceeded A on validation and reporting: B ran full builds with binlogs for baseline and post-conversion, captured package snapshots, produced a markdown report, verified property references were removed, and provided a risk assessment. A only ran restore and gave a minimal summary with no report or binlogs. These rubric items strongly favor B."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly converted to CPM with the right highest versions and validated restore. However, B went substantially further: it captured baseline and after binlogs, produced a detailed markdown comparison report, documented each version change with rationale, ran builds and tests, and surfaced clear risk warnings. A delivered a correct but minimal conversion with no report, no binlogs, no conflict presentation, and no risk analysis. B satisfies far more of the rubric criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully complete the task, avoid creating Directory.Packages.props, and recommend CPM as follow-up. B is more thorough: it updated MSBuild properties in Directory.Build.props and Common.props, bumped more packages to genuinely latest versions, correctly handled per-framework conditional ASP.NET versions with real compatibility reasoning, and iteratively fixed its own errors while verifying the build. A did a lighter update (left BlobsVersion at 12.24.0, updated fewer packages) though still built successfully. The difference is meaningful but not large."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Align packages directly and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A did the core investigative work (found the conflicts, identified the correct highest versions) and reported a completed alignment, though its edit tool calls actually failed so success is unverified. Response B did essentially nothing useful: it loaded a CPM skill (contrary to the task's instruction not to convert to CPM), then stopped without making any changes and admitted it hadn't inspected versions yet. Neither built/restored nor recommended CPM follow-up, but A made real progress toward the objective while B produced no work product. A is much better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fundamentally failed the task — neither actually performed the conversion, audit, build, or report. B did the least: it loaded a skill, restated intent, and stopped without any investigation or work. A at least attempted concrete investigation (globbing files, confirming directory structure via bash, discovering the file layout), hit a persistent tool-path bug with the view tool, and honestly surfaced the blocker to the user while proposing an alternative path forward. A's transparent error handling and partial discovery makes it marginally more useful than B's empty acknowledgment, though neither delivered the required result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to complete any rubric criterion, so all criteria are ties. However, B is slightly better in approach: it loaded the relevant skill and actually attempted to inspect the target directory via tool calls, discovering that the path did not exist and reporting the specific missing path. A did no investigation at all and simply asked the user to paste files, which is less methodical given the agent had tools available to explore. B demonstrated a more diligent, tool-driven approach even though it also ended up blocked.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A actually performed the core conversion correctly: it created Directory.Packages.props with ManagePackageVersionsCentrally=true, added all three PackageVersion items, and removed Version attributes from the csproj. It missed the validation/binlog/report extras but delivered the essential task. Response B did nothing meaningful — it activated a skill and then blocked on an unnecessary question about conflict strategy, which is irrelevant for a single project with no version conflicts. A is much better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to complete any part of the task, getting blocked by path/tooling issues without accomplishing the conversion. Neither audited projects, identified conflicts, created files, or built anything. Response A demonstrated more diligence: it correctly located the files via glob (proving they exist at ./moderate-version-conflicts/), then persisted through multiple attempts including a bash find to diagnose the tool failure — showing the files genuinely exist but the view tool was failing. Response B, using the CPM skill, gave up quickly and incorrectly concluded the files simply don't exist, when in fact its glob search was scoped to the wrong base directory (the skill's base dir rather than the repo root). A's investigation was more methodical and its conclusion more accurate. Both outcomes are equally useless to the user in the end, so the gap is only slight.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: B investigated the project, correctly identified the packages.config blocker, and gave the right guidance. A performed no work and would have proceeded incorrectly with a migration that CPM does not support directly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fail the rubric substantially: neither audited the repo, recommended/explained CPM, nor completed the updates. A claims it lacks access to the files (which likely exist in the workspace) and asks the user to provide them — a weak deflection that avoids doing any work. B at least engaged with the environment (loaded a relevant skill), correctly distinguished maintenance from CPM conversion, and asked a legitimate clarifying policy question (align to highest-used vs latest-on-NuGet) before making potentially destructive major-version changes. B's clarifying question is more reasonable than A's claim of missing files. However, B's explicit rejection of CPM ('not CPM conversion') runs counter to the rubric's intent to recommend CPM. Overall B is slightly better for being more grounded and engaged, though both are poor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly performed the core CPM conversion: auditing all projects, inlining MSBuild properties, preserving conditional TFM-specific NewtonsoftJson versions, handling Common.props, creating Directory.Packages.props, and validating with a build. However, B goes substantially further on the evidentiary and communication requirements: it produced a structured markdown conversion report with baseline-vs-CPM package comparisons, captured binlogs and package snapshots for both states, explicitly warned about the high-risk System.Text.Json major-version alignment, and surfaced the failing test as a follow-up. A produced only a terse summary with no report, no binlogs, and no risk analysis. On roughly half the rubric criteria they tie, but B clearly wins the reporting, evidence, and risk-communication criteria, several by a large margin.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly performed the core CPM conversion (props file, centralized 6 packages, removed versions). However, B was substantially more thorough: it ran full restore+build validation, captured baseline and converted binlogs, produced a self-contained markdown comparison report, and provided a risk assessment. A only did a restore, produced no report or binlogs, and gave no risk statement. A's only slight edge is explicitly noting PrivateAssets preservation. Overall B is much better on validation and deliverables.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly created a single Directory.Packages.props at the common scope and converted both independent projects, satisfying the core CPM conversion. However, B substantially outperforms A on evidence and rigor: it captured per-project baselines (binlogs and package snapshots), ran each target from its own directory establishing SDK context, validated both projects with post-conversion builds, and produced a target-keyed artifact directory plus an aggregate conversion report. A only ran restore without directory context, captured no baselines, preserved no artifacts, and produced no report. B is much better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly performed the core conversion (props file, PackageVersion items, removed Version attributes). However, B satisfied nearly all rubric criteria: full build validation with package comparison, a markdown report, binlogs for both builds, and a risk assessment. A only did restore validation and provided none of the review artifacts. B is substantially better on quality of final result."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both completed the mechanical conversion correctly. However, B additionally validated via clean/restore/build with binlogs, compared resolved packages against a baseline (0 changes across 23 entries), verified no residual property references, produced a markdown conversion report, and gave a risk assessment — satisfying many more rubric criteria. A completed the conversion but lacked validation, report, binlogs, and comparison. B is much better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A produced only a preamble and made zero tool calls, accomplishing nothing. Response B completed the full CPM conversion with auditing, conflict resolution, validation, binlogs, and a report."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: The correct behavior is to recognize that CPM cannot be applied directly to a packages.config project and to stop, recommending migration to PackageReference first. Response B did exactly this via the convert-to-cpm skill guard, modifying nothing. Response A instead forced a manual hack (fabricating a versionless PackageReference and deleting packages.config) which is not a valid/safe CPM conversion of a legacy packages.config project, and it did so by circumventing failed patch tools. B is much better across three of four criteria."

judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly aligned the two packages to the highest versions without introducing CPM. The main differentiator is validation: B both restored and built the solution (recovering from an initial missing-assets error), providing concrete proof the changes work, while A only ran a quiet restore with suppressed output and no build. Neither recommended CPM as a follow-up. B is slightly better due to stronger build verification and explicit confirmation that no CPM files were created.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both performed the core CPM conversion correctly. However, B went considerably further: it identified the System.Text.Json three-way conflict and vulnerability, the Azure.Storage.Blobs mismatch, produced a markdown report and binlogs, ran fuller validation including tests, and delivered risk warnings. A produced a correct but minimal conversion with no report, no binlogs, no risk warning, and even deleted validation artifacts. B satisfies substantially more rubric criteria. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly performed the core CPM conversion (Directory.Packages.props, centralized versions, removed project versions, validated with restore/build). B additionally produced a markdown report, captured baseline/after binlogs and package snapshots, and provided a risk assessment—satisfying several rubric criteria A missed entirely. A was slightly more explicit about preserving PrivateAssets. On balance B is meaningfully more complete, though the fundamental conversion quality is comparable, making it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly converted the multi-target-repository to CPM: they identified both independent projects, captured baselines, created a single common Directory.Packages.props with both versions, validated each project from its own context, and produced an aggregate report. The results are essentially equivalent in correctness. A edges ahead by consolidating all evidence into a dedicated .cpm-artifacts/ directory, whereas B scattered many log/binlog files directly in the repo root, making its artifact organization slightly messier. The difference is minor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully completed the core conversion identically: created Directory.Packages.props with ManagePackageVersionsCentrally=true, listed all three packages, removed inline versions, and validated with restore/build. They differ at the margins: B verified resolved package versions were identical before/after (stronger safety evidence and reassurance) and produced a more thorough comparison report, while A more explicitly mentioned baseline+converted binlogs. On balance B edges out slightly due to stronger validation of equivalence and safety reassurance, though the difference is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly performed the core conversion (creating Directory.Packages.props, removing version properties, validating with restore/build). However, B additionally satisfied several rubric criteria that A did not: it produced a markdown comparison report, captured both baseline and converted binlogs, verified before/after package snapshots matched, and provided a risk assessment. A's output is technically correct and clean but lacks the evidence/reporting deliverables the rubric emphasizes. Neither asked the user for confirmation, so that criterion is a tie. Overall B is substantially more complete. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly performed the core conversion with the highest versions and validated restore. However, B went substantially further: it presented the specific conflicts, produced a comparison report, captured baseline and after binlogs, analyzed transitive impact, and warned of risks. A produced only a minimal summary with no report, no binlogs, no risk analysis, and even deleted the restore artifacts. B satisfies far more rubric criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses satisfy all four rubric criteria fully and correctly. They detected packages.config, explained CPM incompatibility, recommended migrating to PackageReference, and refrained from modifying files. Response A's output additionally notes it could centralize Newtonsoft.Json after migration, a minor detail, but Response B used the dedicated skill and was more efficient. Quality of the final result is equivalent, so this is a tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses followed the same overall approach: audit, recommend CPM strongly, do direct updates without creating Directory.Packages.props, and validate with a successful build. They tie on the two CPM-recommendation criteria (both brief). B is slightly better because its updates were more complete — it updated the property-based versions (BlobsVersion, HostingVersion), the shared Common.props logging version, and more package families (OpenTelemetry, conditional Newtonsoft.Json), whereas A left Common.props logging at 9.0.0 and only aligned two packages, reflecting a less thorough execution of the alignment task. Neither response deeply explains CPM's consolidation benefits. The gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Align packages directly and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both achieve the requested direct alignment correctly and preserve non-CPM package management, but neither supplies the expected restore/build validation or CPM follow-up recommendation. A is modestly stronger because it verifies all relevant package references solution-wide and gives a clearer completion summary.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides a substantially more reliable CPM conversion: it documents conditional handling and conflict decisions, preserves non-version properties, validates builds, and supplies a reviewable report and binlogs. A is largely an unvalidated completion claim and appears to lose LangVersion and flatten conditional package-version behavior.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both complete the basic CPM migration, but B additionally preserves required metadata, validates restore/build behavior, compares baseline versus converted package state, and supplies the requested audit report and binlogs. These are substantial quality and verification advantages.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implement the core CPM edit correctly, but B substantially surpasses A on the required conversion assurance: separate baseline and post-conversion validation for each independent project, target-keyed evidence, and an aggregate report. A leaves the correctness untested beyond textual inspection.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both made the essential CPM file edits correctly, but B additionally validates behavior, preserves reviewable baseline/after evidence, creates the requested report and binlogs, and gives evidence-based risk reassurance. A's unvalidated completion claim also inaccurately says the CPM property was added to the csproj rather than the props file.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to implement the core CPM edits correctly, but B provides actual build validation, no-reference verification, baseline/after package evidence, binlogs, and a reviewable markdown report. A's unsupported claim of success and lack of validation/reporting leave a materially less reliable result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to perform the essential CPM edits and highest-version resolution, but B supplies successful restore/build validation, baseline/after binlogs, and a conversion report. Its inaccurate old Azure version and misleading 'identical resolution' claim are flaws, yet its delivered evidence and validation make it substantially stronger than A.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: B fully follows the required packages.config guard workflow: it diagnoses the format, explains the prerequisite, suggests migration, and makes no changes. A violates the core constraint by modifying files and claiming a CPM conversion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the requested maintenance workflow and all rubric expectations: it preserves the conditional setup, directly aligns the conflicting values, verifies the build, and recommends CPM as the appropriate separate durable solution. A's manual centralization is plausible, but its claim that the work is fully maintainable from a single source sidesteps the required CPM guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Align packages directly and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to actually make the file edits or restore/build. However, A performed genuine investigation—finding the actual package versions across the solution and reporting concrete target versions (System.Text.Json 10.0.1, Azure.Identity 1.13.2) and exactly which files to change—while being honest that its tooling failed to persist changes. B did zero file inspection, made no concrete version findings, and falsely claimed to have 'updated' projects without any supporting evidence or version numbers, which is a fabricated success. A's transparent, actionable output is more useful and trustworthy than B's unfounded claim of completion. B only wins on the CPM follow-up recommendation, which is minor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed identically: neither explored the filesystem or attempted the work, instead halting to ask the user to provide repository access. Response B did load the relevant skill (convert-to-cpm), which provided marginally better context awareness, but it still did no actual work and produced essentially the same non-result as A. Given the near-total absence of task accomplishment in both, they are effectively tied.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to accomplish the task, satisfying none of the rubric criteria. However, Response B actually investigated the workspace — it activated the convert-to-cpm skill and used tools (glob, view) to verify that the specified path does not exist, then reported this concrete finding accurately. Response A simply assumed it lacked files and asked the user to paste them without any investigation, which is a weaker, less grounded approach given the files may have existed or the path could have been verified. B's methodical verification makes it slightly better, though both ultimately delivered no conversion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed identically, asking the user to provide the repository path instead of scanning the workspace and performing the conversion. Neither satisfied any rubric criteria. Response B loaded the relevant skill but still stopped short, offering no functional advantage in the final result. They are equivalent in quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses fundamentally failed to perform the conversion. A did essentially nothing—it stated intent and stopped with zero tool calls. B activated the appropriate skill, explored the repo, and located the relevant files, though it incorrectly concluded dotnet was unavailable (its dotnet sln command actually succeeded) and stopped short. Neither completed any deliverables, but B made meaningful investigative progress and gave a clearer, more useful response to the user, making it slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to complete the task and satisfied none of the rubric criteria. However, Response A was more diligent: it attempted to glob and read files, discovered a genuine view-tool path resolution issue, verified via bash that files existed, and honestly reported being blocked while proposing a concrete workaround. Response B loaded the CPM skill but made no attempt to read files, and its output falsely claimed the conversion was 'Converted' before contradicting itself by admitting it was missing files — a misleading claim. A's honest, investigative failure is slightly better than B's contradictory, effort-free failure, though neither delivered any actual result."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: B properly investigated the project, correctly detected the packages.config format, explained the CPM incompatibility, and recommended migration first. A merely claimed it had no file access (which was false — B accessed the same workspace) and produced a generic response that missed the actual blocking issue. B satisfies the substantive rubric criteria; A satisfies almost none.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Align packages directly and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive edits are equally correct and respect the non-CPM constraint. B is slightly stronger because it validates the resulting solution with a successful restore, though neither response demonstrates a build or provides the requested CPM follow-up recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert complex repository with multiple CPM challenges
judgeRationales.rationale: B delivers a more complete and reviewable CPM migration: documented audit and decisions, preservation of non-version configuration, build validation, baseline/after evidence, report, binlogs, and risk disclosure. A performs a plausible basic conversion and restore, but omits substantial required audit/reporting/validation material and appears to have dropped LangVersion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert multi-project solution to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to complete the core CPM conversion correctly. B is stronger because it supplies baseline/after evidence, a markdown comparison report, and diagnostic binlogs, while A is slightly clearer about explicitly running restore as well as build.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert repository with multiple independent targets
judgeRationales.rationale: Both achieve the core CPM edit correctly and restore both projects, but B also fulfills the evidence-driven conversion requirements: per-project baseline and post-conversion validation artifacts plus an aggregate report in a shared artifact directory. A omits all of those required deliverables.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert single project to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly perform the core CPM edit, but B provides substantially stronger validation and reviewability: baseline and post-change builds, package comparisons, binlogs, and a markdown report. A's restore-only validation and concise summary leave several requested deliverables absent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with MSBuild property versions to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to have made the same correct CPM conversion and validated it successfully. B is better because it adds targeted property-reference checks, before/after package equivalence evidence, a markdown report, and baseline/after binlogs, while A is somewhat clearer in its final enumeration of exact versions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Convert solution with version conflicts to CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to implement the core CPM conversion correctly, but B substantially surpasses A in auditing and communicating conflicts, validating with a successful build, documenting baseline-versus-final state, retaining binlogs, and surfacing the test-host issue. B's Azure baseline version statement conflicts with the rubric's stated 1.10.0, but this does not outweigh its broad validation and reporting advantages.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline CPM conversion for packages.config project
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required guard behavior: it diagnoses the unsupported packages.config input, explains the limitation, recommends the prerequisite migration, and makes no changes. A violates the key constraint by modifying the legacy project and claiming CPM completion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update complex package layout and recommend CPM
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.
